analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties for employers who don't pay workers all their wages.
analysis.headline: The Wage Theft Prevention and Wage Recovery Act was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets wage theft — when employers fail to pay the minimum wage or overtime, require off-the-clock work, misclassify workers, or withhold tips. It would require employers to give new hires written terms of employment, issue itemized paystubs, and pay departing workers within two weeks. It would let workers recover up to triple the wages stolen, extend the time limit for suing from two years to four, stop employers from forcing workers into arbitration over wage claims, and let criminal prosecutors go after repeat offenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are underpaid, especially low-wage workers in industries like food service, retail, construction, and janitorial work. The bill's own findings cite surveys showing large shares of low-wage workers experience wage violations, with women, immigrants, and Black workers hit hardest. Workers who win back wages could recover two to three times the amount owed plus interest, would get paystubs showing how their pay was calculated, could inspect their employer's payroll records, and could take four years (five for willful violations) to sue instead of two.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to be paid the rate stated in an employment contract or union agreement, not just the legal minimum wage.
Requires employers to give workers itemized paystubs, written pay terms at hire, and final payment within 14 days of a job ending — with added daily pay for late final checks.
Raises recoverable damages from 1x to 2x (and 3x for retaliation cases) the wages owed, plus interest, and lengthens the time to sue from 2 years to 4 (5 for willful violations).
Bars employers from using pre-dispute arbitration agreements to strip workers of their right to sue in court, including in collective wage claims.

Requires the Labor Department to refer willful wage theft, record falsification, and retaliation cases to the Justice Department for prosecution, and increases civil fines to up to $10,000 per affected employee for repeat violations.
Authorizes $50 million a year in grants so community organizations and legal aid groups can educate workers about their rights and help them recover stolen wages.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who don't currently pay what they owe, including businesses in industries where wage-and-hour compliance runs below 50% by the bill's own findings. All covered employers would face new paperwork: disclosure statements, itemized paystubs, and five years of accessible payroll records, with fines for falling short. The federal government would fund the grant program through appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small businesses, which would need systems to produce detailed itemized paystubs, initial disclosure statements, and keep records employees can inspect for up to five years.

If an employer fails to produce complete records, the worker's own account of hours and pay would become a legally presumed fact the employer can only rebut with clear and convincing evidence — a rule that could penalize sloppy bookkeeping as harshly as actual theft.

Doubling and tripling damages plus mandatory criminal referrals could raise litigation exposure and settlement costs even for employers acting in good faith who make an honest mistake about hours or classification.
The $50 million annual grant program would be federal spending that could be challenged as a subsidy to advocacy organizations, since labor unions and nonprofits are among eligible grant recipients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits go directly to workers who were legally owed money and didn't receive it, and the bill's own findings cite studies estimating wage theft costs workers more than $15 billion a year and pushes tens of thousands of families into poverty. The main costs are real but ordinary: paperwork and recordkeeping for every employer, and heavier financial risk for violators. The record-penalty presumption is the most aggressive design choice and could be unfair in edge cases where records are lost but no theft occurred. On the whole, the costs fall on employers in proportion to their legal obligations, while the gains go to workers in the lowest-paid jobs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, and expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on July 27, 2017, with 22 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction; that was the bill's only action.
The bill never advanced beyond committee and received no further action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
By the end, the bill had 25 cosponsors, all Democrats and no Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers are better off because the bill died: no paystub mandates, no higher damages, no extended statute of limitations, and no arbitration ban, so the risk and cost of wage violations stays where it was.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; it died in committee without a recorded vote, so the partisan split is inferred from sponsorship rather than a roll call.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (food service, retail, janitorial, construction subcontractors)
industries.note: These employers face the bill's sharpest edges: mandatory paystubs and disclosures, treble damages, longer lawsuits, a bar on arbitration clauses, and criminal referral for willful violations. Their interest in avoiding these rules runs against the workers seeking the wages they were already owed.

industries.industry: Staffing and labor subcontracting firms that misclassify workers
industries.note: The bill targets misclassification of employees as independent contractors or as exempt from overtime, a core cost-saving practice in this segment, and adds recordkeeping penalties that would make the practice riskier.

The bill's findings note that noncompliant competitors gain an unfair cost advantage; stronger enforcement levels the field for employers who already pay correctly, though they still bear new paystub and recordkeeping paperwork.

industries.industry: Nonprofit legal aid, community organizations, and labor unions
industries.note: They become eligible for $50 million a year in federal grants to run worker outreach and help employees recover back pay alongside the Labor Department.
